title: one full moon, three stories
hookLine: lanterns, a baby statue bathed in water, temples at dawn: the Buddha's birthday, and more
carry: he was a person who woke up

lines: LANTERNS. A BABY STATUE. WHITE CLOTHES.
cards: Lotus lanterns strung across a street in Seoul. A small statue of a baby, one hand pointing up, standing in a bowl of flowers while people line up to pour water over it.
Families dressed in white at a temple in Sri Lanka before sunrise. Many of them will tell you it's the Buddha's birthday. Some will tell you it's more than that.
Same festival, told differently. First, a guess.

teach.b: Vesak takes its name from a spring month in the old Indian calendar.

In many Theravada countries, like Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar, its full moon marks three things at once: the Buddha's birth, his awakening and his death. Tradition says all three fell on that same full moon.
In Japan, the birthday has its own flower festival in April, and across much of East Asia his awakening and death are remembered on other days of the year.
Different calendars, the same life. The water poured over the baby statue recalls a story: when he was born, streams of water fell from the sky to bathe him. And who is everyone celebrating?
Buddha isn't a name. It's a title, from a word meaning to wake up. In one old story, a man follows his footprints and asks: are you a god?
A human being? No again. Then what are you?
Remember me, he says, as awake.

teach.h: HE WAS A PERSON WHO WOKE UP.
teach.b: Not a god, by his own account: a person who woke up.

how: On Vesak, Buddhists in many Theravada countries visit temples, keep the precepts, give food, hang lanterns and remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and death together; in East Asia the Buddha's birthday is marked with lanterns and by pouring water or sweet tea over a statue of the infant Buddha, with his awakening and death remembered on other days.

games.q: one festival, many places — tap the pairs.
p: marked together in many Theravada lands
water from the sky at his birth
a title: one who woke up

s: Vesak marks only the Buddha's birthday, everywhere
in many Theravada countries it marks his birth, awakening and death together; elsewhere they fall on different days.
Buddha is a title, not a name
it means one who woke up. his name, tradition says, was Siddhattha Gotama.
asked if he was a god, the Buddha said yes
asked if he was a god, a spirit or a human, he said no each time: remember me as awake.

games.q: a man follows the Buddha's footprints and asks: are you a god? a spirit? a human being? what does he answer, in the story?
games.why: remember me as awake: a buddha. not a claim to be a god, and not quite 'just a man' either.

games.q: put the three moments Vesak remembers in order.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, picture a single lantern being lit. On the second, bring to mind one person whose life lit something in yours.
On the third, let yourself be glad they were here.

wordCard.voice: Vesak. One spring full moon for his birth, his awakening and his death, told differently in different places. Sixth word.

orig.note: Pali: Vesākha, a spring month; Sanskrit Vaiśākha. Thailand calls the festival Visakha Bucha.

carryVoice: Your line: he was a person who woke up. That's who the lanterns are for. Day six, done.
